editorial:
The Mummy Strikes is described by Wikipedia as the fourteenth of seventeen animated Technicolor Superman shorts. Famous Studios made it for Paramount, and it was released in February 1943. Isadore Sparber directed, Jay Morton wrote the story, Sam Buchwald produced, and Winston Sharples and Sammy Timberg are listed in Wikipedia's infobox for the music. Creators look for these shorts because the animation is lavish and the set-piece scenes are easy to clip.

The open question is Superman, not only the print. For a 1943 film, a renewal would have had to be filed in 1970 or 1971. An earlier look at the 1971 volume found no renewal, but the method was not recorded, so we do not rely on it. We have not checked the 1970 volume of the printed Catalog of Copyright Entries. Even if the print is free, the Superman character may carry separate rights that could be a risk for any new work that uses him. We have not confirmed that with a source. Reusing the cartoon unchanged is a different question from making new Superman material.
faq: Is The Mummy Strikes free to reuse?

Not confirmed yet. A renewal would have been due in 1970 or 1971. Our earlier look at the 1971 Catalog of Copyright Entries found no renewal, but we did not record the method, so it is unverified, and the 1970 volume is unchecked. The Superman character may carry separate rights from the print. We have not confirmed that.
Does the music have its own copyright?

The soundtrack was recorded as part of the film, so it should share the print's status. Wikipedia's infobox lists Winston Sharples and Sammy Timberg for the music, which we have not checked against the title card. We have not confirmed a separate music registration either way.
